meta.workDescription: 1. PURPOSE: This outline aims to provide Initial/Annual Recurring Job Safety Training and Job Specific Training to employees assigned to the Warner Robins Air Logistics Complex (WR-ALC). Supervisors will provide and document safety training to all newly assigned employees on the hazards of their job before they start work and immediately when there is a change in equipment, processes, work environment, or safety, fire, and health requirements. The supervisor shall cover all aspects of workplace safety with respect to physical safety, fire safety, and health hazards. This JSTO has two sections; Mandatory Items and Shop Specific Items. Each area may be tailored to adequately address the specific concerns of an employee's workplace. Once training is completed, annotate training on the DAF Form 1286, Safety Education-Training Class Roster, or equivalent form IAW WR-ALCI 91-205, Documentation of Safety Training, Attachment 3. Route documentation to the squadron training office or group training manager for an update in Training Scheduling System Production Acceptance Certification (TSS/PAC). Supervisors will review and update the JSTO annually and when there is a change in equipment, processes, or safety, fire, and health requirements, and document the review on this page. Reference: DAFI 91-202, Chapter 14 and AFI 91-202 AFMCSUP, Chapter 14.
meta.hazardAnalysis:
JHAs are conducted on all work processes, where appropriate, to identify potential hazards, determine appropriate Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) and include preventative measures in procedures to mitigate hazards. Part of the JHA process overlaps Bioenvironmental (BE) efforts to link tasks to hazards and identifying Occupational and Environmental Health PPE requirements. The JHA shall involve BE to avoid duplication of effort and to ensure proper awareness of process changes. Note: A JHA is not required when existing guidance adequately ensures all safety requirements of an operation or process.
Hazardous Noise: Some tools and equipment used to perform assigned tasks generate hazardous noise. Employees exposed to high noise levels will familiarize themselves with the damaging effects that high noise levels can cause to the human body and wear the proper ear protection to prevent damage. Hearing protection is required in all noise hazard areas and will be worn when using equipment such as band saws, sanders, pneumatic grinders, pneumatic drills, and other noise-producing tools and powered equipment.
Handling of Hazardous Chemicals/Waste: PPE will be used while handling all hazardous chemicals, including adhesives, primers, paints, methylene chloride, fillers, glues, composites, and sealants in accordance with the appropriate Safety Data Sheet (SDS). Adequate ventilation may be required while handling chemicals. Employees shall read and understand the appropriate and most current SDS and work center HRA before handling any chemical. Employees may obtain SDSs from their supervisor, the pharmacy from which they received the chemicals, or online. All employees will follow proper disposal procedures.
Lifting Heavy Objects: Use mechanical lifting devices to move heavy objects when possible. Always use proper posture when lifting any heavy or bulky object. Always bend at the knees and keep a straight back. Place feet close to the item and apart to maintain balance. Use team lifting when items are too heavy for one person or when items are lifted from an awkward position or location. Always watch for pinch points and be certain to wear proper hand protection. There are three basic methods of lifting, straight back with bent knees, freestyle, and kinetic. Each has advantages and limitations. The kinetic method is the most widely accepted and taught because it provides more stability for the worker while reducing the load on the back muscles and intervertebral disk. Safe lifting training is an annual training requirement. The supervisor should brief the following instructions on how to lift correctly:
•
Feet Position: Place feet far enough apart for balance, with one foot to the rear of the object and the other foot slightly ahead of the other and to the side of the object.
•
Body Position: Crouch close to the load. Stay close to the load to minimize strain on the lower back. Before beginning the lift, be sure the back is straight as possible and back muscles are tightened. These steps prepare the body to accept the load.
•
Hand Protection: Pick up materials with a full palm grip. Do not attempt to pick up weights with a fingertip grip. Ensure the load is free of grease or sharp points which could cause injury. Use suitable gloves when necessary.
•
Protect the Back: Always keep the back as straight as possible. It may not be possible to keep the back in the vertical plane but avoid arching the back. Keep the back muscles tightened throughout the duration of the lift. Do not relax the back until the load is released. Bend from the hips and not from the middle of the back.
•
General Principles: With the arms, slide the object toward the body to give it some motion (kinetic energy). At the same time, use the legs to lift the object and bring the back to a vertical position. Keep the object close to the body while lifting.
•
Team Lifting: When required to manually move heavy or unusually shaped items, always seek and obtain assistance. When two or more people are required to move or carry an object, adjust the load so each person carries an equal part. Test lifts should be made before proceeding. The key to lifts using two or more personnel is to make every move in unison. The supervisor and workers are responsible for assessing all available methods to safely handle materials described above and use mechanical assistance whenever possible.
•
Carrying Methods: Acceptable carrying methods differ, based upon the type of material, distance, and number of workers. Workers should be instructed during initial training in each procedure (for example, neck, shoulder, side tray, two-person, and under-arm carry methods, etc.).
•
Avoid Twisting: Twisting can overload the spine and lead to serious injury. Make sure feet, knees, and torso are pointed in the same direction when lifting.
Metal/Fiberglass Handling Hazards: Any time employees work around metal or fiberglass, they are subject to cuts, nicks, and scrapes. Be cautious of the bleed out from resin which can leave a sharp edge which presents a laceration hazard. Always deburr the edges of the material to take the razor edge off, and always wear gloves when handling sharp materials.
Air Borne Dust: Employees may be required to sand a variety of sealants, corrosion, and composites. Employees should utilize sanding booths to minimize dust in the shop area. When sanding specific components, employees must wear a respirator and eye protection. Refer to the shop workplace HRA for guidance. If controls are absent or condition of controls are unknown, consult the local Bioenvironmental Engineering (BEE) office or WR-ALC/SE Staff.
High Temperatures: Employees may be required to operate portable cookers, autoclaves, and ovens to cook/bond repairs. Always wear the proper PPE to prevent burns.
Electrical Equipment: Ensure machines powered by electricity are properly disconnected from the power source before performing equipment maintenance. Employees will use a variety of heat lamps, blow dryers, portable cookers, and heat blankets. Always check for frayed electrical cords or damaged plugs. Ensure that malfunctioning equipment has been properly Locked Out and Tagged Out and only authorized employees repair electrical equipment or removed from service and disposed of correctly. Refer to 29 CFR 1910, Subpart S and DAFMAN 91-203, Chapter 8.
Slippery Surfaces: The floors and aisles can pose a potential slipping hazard when a spill or rain occurs. Always wipe up non-hazardous spills immediately. Oil leaks from forklifts and tugs can also be a slipping hazard in the shop; always clean up any spill or leak immediately. Always use caution when in areas where wet or small media is introduced in a process.
Congested Areas: Congested areas have the potential to create falling/tripping hazards. Be aware of these hazards and clean all areas during and after maintenance. Route lines and hoses through areas less traveled and keep the tops of fixtures and cabinets free from loose tools or parts. Keep walkways clear and free of obstructions.
For additional information, refer to 29 CFR § 1910, Subpart D; DAFMAN 91-203, Ch. 7.; and WR-ALCI 91-203, Para. 2.4.1.
Hangar Doors and Overhead Doors: Always stand clear when operating doors. Never enter or exit while a door is in motion. Hazardous areas include crush and pinch points between structural beams and the doors. Highlight hazardous areas such as crush and pinch points that cannot be eliminated by engineering controls or mechanical safeguards with colored paint and signs. Reference WR-ALCI 91-203, Ch. 5; and Attachment 4, HANGAR DOOR SAFETY INSPECTION GUIDE
Vehicles: A golf cart, pick-up truck, or a passenger van/car can be operated with a valid state driver’s license. An operator MUST have an AF Form 483, Certificate of Competency, to operate any vehicles on the AMXG industrial ramp or the flightline. Reference WR-ALCI 24-300, Para. 2.4.13 for additional information.
Propeller and Jet Aircraft Blasts: Employees will stay within the prescribed safe distance of 250 feet from the blasts of the aircraft. All run-up areas will be kept free of debris and foreign material. During engine operations, employees will remain at least 25 feet from intakes and propellers. Only authorized employees will be in the operating area. Reference DAFMAN 91-203, Para. 24.10.3 for additional information.
Propeller and Jet Intake Hazards: During aircraft run-up, all employees will avoid danger areas marked by the red strip on the aircraft/engine and/or fuselage. Employees will stay at least 25 feet from the front of the propellers and intakes. C-130 propellers present a hazard whether in operation or static. If bleed air is applied to the aircraft, employees will not be in the vicinity of (or go through) the static propeller arc. Employees will not stand in line with the stripe that designates the plane of the turbine wheel and propeller operation, which is painted on the fuselage or engine nacelles of aircraft. WARNING: Danger Area. Personnel will not be in the vicinity of or go through the static propeller arc of reciprocating and turboprop aircraft or helicopters unless necessary in performing duties. Employees should always use caution to prevent head injury from ramming unnoticed propellers.
Suspended Loads: Aircraft tail sections, engines, and wing sections have been dropped while suspended by hoists, cranes, or jacks, causing extensive damage and, in some cases, injury. Never stand under a suspended load. Affected employees will thoroughly inspect the equipment suspending loads before each use, safety rules, instructions, and will adhere to IAW DAFMAN 91-203, Chapter 12, Materials Handling Equipment. The wearing of appropriate hard hats is mandatory when working around cranes/hoists. Only authorized personnel will remain in the vicinity of the operation. Office Hazards: Each employee is responsible for policing their workplace to reduce the potential for storage and housekeeping-related injuries. Filing cabinets will not be top loaded with heavy items leaving the bottom drawers empty; this creates a tipping hazard. Desk and cabinet drawers will not be left open and unattended. Employees will position all phones, computers, and electrical cords to prevent tripping or obstruction hazards. The last person out of the office will check to ensure that items are turned off and that no conditions exist that could cause damage if left on.
Office Ergonomics: The scientific purpose of ergonomics is to fit the work to the worker. Workstation design should be tailored to provide good lighting, sitting position, and keyboard height. These features provide less strain when working at computer workstations. Repetitive tasks such as typing may create physical problems. To avoid such problems, alternate tasks to prevent the over-exertion of a particular body part or series of parts. Schedule daily tasks with this in mind. Consult the local Ergonomics Office or WR-ALC/SE personnel to schedule an ergonomics assessment and suggest solutions for modifying the work to the worker.
Portable Ladders: Portable ladders are used in a variety of Air Force environments. To ensure employees are minimally exposed to the potential hazards of portable ladders, the following foundational training plan was developed. Refer to manufacture guidance for additional information and training. The supervisor may add additional information as required.
Falls are the primary hazard associated with the use of portable ladders. Falls may result from several unsafe acts and conditions such as:

- Ladders being set on unstable surfaces.
- Personnel reaching too far out to the sides of the ladder.
 - Personnel standing too high to maintain balance.
- Personnel using defective ladders (e.g., broken rails, missing hardware)
- Improvising and using a make-shift ladder.
- Personnel carrying materials in their hands while ascending or descending a ladder or descending with their back to the ladder.
- Using a ladder with conductive side rails while working on electrical circuits.
Thorough visual inspections of ladders will be made by the supervisor when the ladder is initially received and prior to being placed in service. Workers will perform a visual inspection prior to each use. Defects or damage to look for include:
- Evidence the ladder was exposed to excessive heat (such as in a fire) or to corrosive substances.
- Side rails, steps, rungs, or related hardware that are cracked, split, or deformed.
- Nonskid base material that is loose or missing. Metal and metal-reinforced single and extension ladders will be equipped with safety shoes, spurs, spikes, or combinations thereof to prevent slipping.
- Metal and metal reinforced ladders that are not marked for electrical hazards.
- Ladders not marked with safety use instructions by the manufacturer shall be stenciled, “DANGER — DO NOT USE AROUND ELECTRICAL EQUIPMENT,” in 2-inch-high red letters or the largest letters the surface will allow (minimum letter size is 1 inch).
- Rungs or steps on metal or fiberglass ladders that are not corrugated, knurled, dimpled, or in some way made skid resistant.
- Ladders with broken or missing steps, rungs or cleats, broken side rails, or other defects. Ladders with these defects will not be used.
- Pulleys, cables, and ropes which bind or are frayed.
Employees who use ladders with working height of 4 foot or more will be adequately trained in the care and use of different types of ladders. The supervisor or a designated trainer will conduct this training when a worker is first assigned. All training will include hands-on instruction to include inspection of ladders for defects, possible electrocution hazards, proper positioning, and placement of ladders for various job sites. Additional information for ladders can be found in DAFMAN 91-203, paragraph 7.4.
meta.trafficSafetyNotes:
Requirements of Air Force Traffic Safety Program (Reference: AFI 91-207).
•
Seat belts will be worn when operating or riding in any motor vehicle on RAFB. Drivers are responsible for ensuring that passengers fasten their seatbelts.
•
Hands free cell phones are authorized for use while driving on RAFB, all other cell phone use will require the driver to pull over and stop the vehicle.
•
All bicycle riders on RAFB will be required to always wear appropriate head gear.
•
Speed limits are typically posted for all roads on RAFB, however, if no signs are posted 25 mph will be adhered to.
•
Be vigilant of the pedestrian cross walks while operating a vehicle on RAFB and stop whenever pedestrians are present in the cross walks.

meta.evacuation:
Emergency action and fire prevention plans applicable to the workplace:
- Brief the location and use of emergency and fire protection equipment (i.e., alarms, AEDs, and extinguishers). Refer to figure 2.
- In the event of a fire, all personnel will report to their designated assembly area so that every employee is accounted for. Failure to do so may result in a false report to the fire department.
- Fire extinguishers and fire alarm pull stations are located throughout the areas. A fire alarm is always near doors that open exterior to the building. Refer to emergency management plans for additional information. To activate the fire alarm, pull station, grab the handle and pull down sharply.
- Only use fire extinguishers to fight small containable fires. Refer to the acronym PASS to properly use a fire extinguisher:
  - Pull the pin located on the handle.
  - Aim the hose at the base of the fire.
  - Squeeze the handle to dispense agent.
  - Sweep the hose from side to side until the fire has been extinguished.
- Extreme caution must be used when fighting any fire regardless of size. Even after successfully extinguishing a fire, contact the Fire Department and advise them of the fire. Additional training for all types of fire and all types of fire extinguisher is available through the fire prevention office.
- Know installation siren signals. Listen to the radio, television, public address system, or Security Police vehicle PA system for type of emergency and action required. Be prepared to take shelter.

meta.activeShooter: Active Shooter Response. Escape, Barricade, or Fight. During an active shooter incident, there are three response options: escape, barricade, and/or fight. These choices are not in any particular order and there are no requirements to progress through one option before selecting another. The decision whether to escape, barricade, or fight is based on two factors: (1) proximity to the shooter, and (2) the accessibility of escape routes. Refer to AFTTP 3-4.6, Air Force Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures.
